results.name: Scale AI just hired a Google Cloud security chief as CEO: Does that tell you everything about where its money will come from? — TFN
results.content:
- Francis deSouza will become Scale AI’s CEO on August 10. He previously led Google Cloud’s security division.
- This move comes as Scale AI shifts its focus to government and enterprise contracts, moving beyond its earlier AI-lab data deals.
- DeSouza’s last CEO role at Illumina ended after a proxy battle led by Carl Icahn, demonstrating his experience handling tough situations.  
Instead of picking another founder, [Scale AI,](https://scale.com/) a San Francisco-based AI infrastructure and applications company, chose a security executive. [Francis deSouza](https://www.linkedin.com/in/francisdesouza), who will take over as CEO on August 10, 2026, according to the [company’s announcement](https://scale.com/blog/scale-ai-appoints-francis-desouza-as-ceo).  
deSouza spent the last year and a half as chief operating officer at Google Cloud and president of security products, managing Google Cloud’s security portfolio, threat intelligence, and governance during a period of rapid growth. He is also on the board of [Deel.](https://techfundingnews.com/deel-raises-300m-at-17-3b-valuation-ai-global-payroll/)  
This choice shows where Scale AI’s board expects the company’s future revenue to come from.
## A new focus on government and enterprise markets  
Scale AI started out by providing labelled data to help train advanced AI models for companies like OpenAI, Google, and Meta.  
Recently, though, the company has highlighted new enterprise clients such as BP and Mayo Clinic, as well as additional partnerships with US and international governments. These contracts focus on trust and compliance, so Scale AI needs leaders who know how to work with security-focused customers.  
DeSouza brings decades of relevant experience. He became president of products and services at Symantec after it acquired IMlogic, an instant-messaging security firm he founded, in 2006, overseeing more than 15,000 employees. Previously, he co-founded Flash Communications, which Microsoft acquired in 1998. Both companies focused on securing enterprise communications.  
[Alexandr Wang](https://www.linkedin.com/in/alexandrwang), who remains Scale’s chairman, stated that deSouza’s experience serving enterprises and governments at the highest levels of trust and reliability aligns with the company’s increased focus on government and defence contracts, a sector that is attracting significant venture capital investment.  
What we can learn from his past CEO experience: DeSouza joined [Illumina](https://www.illumina.com/), a genomic sequencing company, as president in 2013 and became CEO in 2016. While he was there, revenue grew to over $4.5 billion, and the company expanded to more than 150 countries.
## What Meta’s involvement means for Scale  
DeSouza will be leading a company that is almost half-owned by its biggest customer. Alexandr Wang left Scale to join Meta as part of a [$14.3 billion deal that gave Meta a 49% stake](https://techfundingnews.com/meta-invests-in-scale-ai/), more than a year before this appointment. Jason Droege, who has been interim CEO since Wang left, will help deSouza during the transition.  
It makes sense to hire a leader with a background in security and government if Scale’s growth depends on customers who need to trust the company, regardless of its ties to Meta. This move signals a strategy to find more clients who care about compliance, security, and trust—areas where deSouza has extensive experience.

results.name: Scale AI Review: The Data Labeling Giant That Became America's Defense AI Infrastructure — ChatForest
results.content:
Ten years later, Scale AI has $2 billion in annual revenue growing at 130% year-over-year, a $29 billion valuation, and a [$500 million Pentagon contract awarded in May 2026](https://www.forbes.com/sites/aliciapark/2026/05/06/pentagon-hands-meta-backed-scale-ai-500-million-contract-5-times-last-years-deal-report-says/). Wang himself [left the company in June 2025 to become Meta’s Chief AI Officer](https://techcrunch.com/2025/06/13/scale-ai-confirms-significant-investment-from-meta-says-ceo-alexandr-wang-is-leaving/). The data labeling startup he built is now, quietly, one of the most consequential pieces of AI infrastructure in the United States.
That narrative was directionally accurate, which is why it stuck.  
**Jason Droege**, who became Interim CEO after Wang’s departure in June 2025, was previously Scale’s Chief Strategy Officer and founder of Uber Eats. Droege has operational scale at the level Scale needed — Uber Eats built a global logistics network under extreme timeline pressure. Whether he can carry forward the strategic positioning that Wang established is the open question inside Scale right now.  
Wang himself sits at Meta as Chief AI Officer, heading Meta Superintelligence Labs. He is simultaneously one of Meta’s most senior technical executives and Scale’s most famous alumnus working at its largest investor. The dynamics there are unusual.
## Verdict  
Scale AI is in an uncomfortable transitional position that its strong financials do not fully describe.  
The $2B revenue and 130% growth look exceptional. The $500M Pentagon contract is a remarkable validation of the defense bet. Wang’s instinct that evaluation is a more defensible moat than annotation was correct. Scale Labs and the benchmarking work are genuinely important — good AI evaluation is harder than it looks, and there is real demand for trusted third-party assessment of model quality and safety.  
But the Meta deal restructured Scale’s competitive position in ways that are still playing out. Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, and xAI all walked. The commercial AI training market that Scale dominated in 2023 belongs, increasingly, to Surge/Mercor and to in-house teams. Scale’s defense business is impressive but politically dependent — contracts can be restructured, administrations change, and the DoL investigation adds legal overhang.  
The labor practices issues are serious and unresolved. Paying annotators fractions of cents per task while generating billions in revenue from their work is a material ESG and legal risk, not just bad optics. The active Department of Labor investigation and the psychological harm lawsuit represent genuine exposure.  
And the company is now being run by a CEO who was not the founder, reporting to a board that includes a 49% stakeholder who is also the largest customer. The alignment pressures on Droege are complex.
